title: TA8-14566
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (thereinafter referred to as "the claimant") is a citizen of Cuba claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 The claimant's identity as a national of Cuba is established by the true certified copy of her Cuban passport.2 ALLEGATIONS
A summary of the allegations is as follows:

The claimant is a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX from Cuba. The claimant fears the Cuban regime because she has been labelled politically unreliable because she was perceived to have associated herself with dissidents in Canada during her trip in 2000. She is also believed to have made anti-government statements in the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. In 2000, she tried to get approval from her XXXXX XXXXX to travel to Canada in 2000. Initially, the XXXXX said yes, but later changed her mind and told the claimant she had to apply for approval in writing. The claimant drafted a request in writing for leave from her regular work duties during XXXXX XXXXX and had it delivered by the secretary of the People's Power to her XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant later found out that when the secretary tried to deliver the written request to XXXXX XXXXX, XXXXX refused to accept it because she said that it should have been brought to her by the claimant in person. When the claimant returned to Cuba, she was fired from her job. She appealed the decision and lost. She appealed it to a higher tribunal and lost again. In 2007, she bribed officials of the Ministry of Immigration in order to get an exit permit to leave Cuba and come to Canada. Her son who is in Canada returned to Cuba in 2010 and discovered there are citations outstanding against her in Cuba. The claimant fears that she will be prosecuted for illegal exit and dangerousness and will not have due process of law and will be subjected to other extra-judicial measures, including denial of employment, constant surveillance by the communist authorities, and denial of rations and identity cards.
I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. My reasons are as follows. ANALYSIS Section 96 - Convention Refugee Grounds

The determinative issue in this section 96 analysis is whether the claimant's subjective fear is objectively well-founded, or put another way, whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant will be persecuted by the Cuban authorities by reason of one of the five enumerated Convention grounds. Nexus

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has established a nexus between her subjective fear of persecution and the Convention ground of perceived or imputed political opinion. The claimant indicated that after returning to Cuba from Canada in XXXXX 2000, she was told by her XXXXX XXXXX that she had been fired from her job as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX because she was deemed to be politically unreliable due to the fact that she had made anti-government statements against the principles of the revolution in XXXXX and had associated in Canada with political dissidents opposed to the Cuban government. The claimant testified that the allegations made by her XXXXX XXXXX were not true. However, she did indicate that during XXXXX XXXXX, every three to four months, she had meetings with her fellow XXXXX XXXXX and her XXXXX XXXXX, and that on those occasions she had been critical of the Cuban government's treatment of the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. She said that she had indicated that it was not fair for the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX by being denied programs and opportunities that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX had been able to take advantage of, such as XXXXX XXXXX. She said that she cared deeply for the welfare of XXXXX and that she was only looking out for their best interests. The claimant testified that at no time following these meetings did she suffer any reprisals or disciplinary measures at the hands of her XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant said that she asked the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX should not enjoy the same rights as the other XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant said that her XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX said that the reason for this policy was so that the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX would not share, or infect that minds of other XXXXX XXXXX with the views of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.

I find that what is important is not whether the claimant herself expressed anti-government sentiments, or whether she openly criticized the policies and programs of the Cuban government, or whether she actually associated with political dissidents in Canada in 2000, but whether the authorities in Cuba perceived her actions, or conduct to be tantamount to an expression of political opposition to Castro's regime. It is important to note that her XXXXX XXXXX who was a representative of the Communist party, clearly expressed the views that she perceived the claimant's actions of being outside of Cuba without lawful justification as rendering her to be politically unreliable, as well as her having made statements against the principles of the revolution in XXXXX and having associated with political dissidents in Canada. Well-foundedness of Subjective fear (a) Evidence of Past Persecution:

The definition of Convention refugee is forward looking. However, past persecution is an important indicator of what might happen in the future. In XXXXX 2000, the claimant left Cuba in order to pay a visit to her son in Canada. The claimant testified that she obtained all the requisite approvals from her XXXXX XXXXX, municipality, and officials within the Ministry of XXXXX. She indicated that she was given her exit permission in XXXXX 1999, so that she would be able to travel to Canada during her vacation period, which was when XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. However, the claimant indicated that she was not able to leave Cuba in XXXXX 1999 because the Canadian High Commission in Havana did not issue the visitor's visa until XXXXX 2000. The claimant said that after she got her Canadian visitor's visa she approached her XXXXX XXXXX and showed her the Canadian visa. The claimant said that as soon as she showed the XXXXX her visa, the XXXXX granted her permission to leave Cuba in XXXXX 2000. The claimant said that she took ill and after she returned to XXXXX she asked her XXXXX and legal counsel about what other requirements she would have to meet in order to leave Cuba outside of her vacation period. The claimant said she was told she would have to submit a leave request in writing. The claimant said that before she left, she drafted a request for a period of three months leave and had it delivered by the secretary of the Peope's Power to her XXXXX. The claimant said she later learned, that she was supposed to have delivered this written request for leave in person to the XXXXX XXXXX. She said that she was never told the request had to be delivered in person. The claimant said that when she returned to Cuba in XXXXX 2000, she learned that she had been fired from her job. She said that she had a meeting with her XXXXX XXXXX who told her she was fired because she had left Cuba outside of her vacation period without proper authorization and had thus committed a serious offence. The claimant said that the XXXXX also told her that she had obtained information indicating that she had made statements against principles of the revolution XXXXX and had been associated with political dissidents in Canada when she visited her son. The claimant said that despite having appealed the decision several times, each time the original decision to fire her permanently from her work with the Ministry of XXXXX was upheld. The claimant said that after she was fired she was blacklisted and watched by officials very closely. She said that she was blacklisted by the authorities, and as a direct result, was unable to find any work, despite her numerous attempts to do so. She said that in order to survive, she had to engage in an illegal and underground "moonshine" business. The claimant said that the authorities knew she was involved in this illegal business and had told her on many occasions to stop doing it, but that they ultimately did not have any proof at that time to implicate her. The claimant said that it was through this illegal business that she continued to be employed by a friend after she was fired from her job with the Ministry of XXXXX.

I find that when the claimant resorted to engaging in employment through a friend on the black market, she knew that the activity of bootlegging was illegal in Cuba. Despite that knowledge, the claimant intentionally participated in an activity considered to be illegal according to the laws of Cuba. Since Raul Castro took over power in Cuba, he doubled efforts to curb black market activities that were a drain on the Cuban economy.3 I find that if the claimant were to be punished for having engaged in an illegal activity and black market business that it would not amount to persecution, rather it would constitute a lawful sanction for violating Cuba's laws which have a valid purpose.

I accept that the actions of the Cuban authorities in firing her permanently from her job as a XXXXX XXXXX, blacklisting her so as to prevent her from finding any work, keeping her under surveillance, and stopping her on the street to check her bags, amounts to discrimination on the grounds of the claimant's perceived political opinion. In the particular circumstances of this case, I find that the consequences that the claimant faced did not rise to a level of serious harm or severe discrimination amounting to persecution either individually or cumulatively. Although the claimant had serious difficulty finding any work after she was fired from the Ministry of XXXXX, nonetheless, she was able to rely on the goodwill of a close friend who got her involved in a black market bootlegging operation. It was through this means, according to the claimant, that she was able to survive and provide for herself until she left Cuba for the last time in XXXXX 2008. (b) Risk of Future Persecution:

The claimant testified that in 2006 she started making plans to leave Cuba. She said that in order to get an exit permit, she needed a letter of employment. However, since she had been blacklisted and had been unable to find work since 2000, she said that she had to resort to getting a fraudulent employment letter from a friend in 2006. She said that after her friend gave her this employment letter she approached the Canadian High Commission in Havana to get a temporary visitor's visa to return to Canada, but her application was refused. She said that she presented another application for a visitor's visa to the Canadian High Commission in XXXXX 2007. She said that this time around, she approached another friend of hers who was a XXXXX XXXXX. She said her friend prepared a fraudulent employment letter which enabled her to get an exit permit from the Cuban authorities. She said that in XXXXX 2007, the Canadian High Commission accepted her application and issued her a visitor's visa for Canada. The claimant said that she was not able to travel to Canada until XXXXX 2008, because her son and her daughter-in-law had to deal with a family emergency.

The claimant testified that when she presented the fraudulent employment letter to the Ministry of XXXXX, she had no problem getting an exit permit. The claimant said that her Cuban exit permit was valid until XXXXX, 2008. The claimant said that there was no way to extend her exit permit from abroad in Canada. The claimant said that she believed that she was given this exit permit, despite her past record of violating the laws governing the attendance of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and having been deemed politically unreliable by her XXXXX XXXXX who believed her to have engaged in anti-government behaviour, because all that was needed to get her an exit permit was a letter from a XXXXX XXXXX official. The claimant explained that a letter from a XXXXX official, such as a XXXXX, would be given considerable deference by senior officials of the government when considering whether to permit a Cuban XXXXX XXXXX to leave the country. The claimant presented no persuasive evidence to substantiate her claim that in Cuba all that would be required for a XXXXX XXXXX to be able to obtain an exit permit from the authorities is a letter from XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant also explained that she believed that she was able to get her exit permit, despite her past record, because her previous problems had happened in the distant past, but the employment letter she received from her XXXXX XXXXX friend was recent. The claimant said that she did not know if the Cuban authorities were aware of the fact that she had used illegal means by which to obtain her lawful exit permit from Cuba. She said that if the authorities found out that she had done this that she and the other people who helped her leave the country would go to jail. There is no persuasive evidence to suggest that the authorities in Cuba know that the claimant used illegal means to obtain her exit permit, or that they are highly likely to find out that the claimant used illegal methods to gain her exit from the country.

In the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF), the claimant indicates that another reason why she was able to get an exit permit from the Cuban authorities in 2007, despite her past record of political unreliability and unauthorized departure from the country during the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, was that a friend of hers who worked in the Ministry of the Interior put her in touch with officials in the Ministry of Immigration whom she was able to bribe by giving them perfumes and soaps. I find, given the widespread and pervasive monitoring of private communications and widespread surveillance of daily activities of Cubans, it is implausible that the claimant would have been able to bribe officials within the Ministry of Immigration in order to get an exit permit in the manner in which she has described. Authorities interfered with privacy and engaged in pervasive monitoring of private communications.4 Specialized units of the Ministry of the Interior's state security service are responsible for monitoring, infiltrating, and suppressing opposition political groups. While the constitution provides for the inviolability of a citizen's home and correspondence, official surveillance of private and family affairs by government controlled organizations, such as the Committees for the Defense of the Revolution (CDR), remained pervasive. The government employed physical and electronic surveillance against political opponents, interfered in the lives of citizens, and employed a wide range of social controls to discover and discourage nonconformity. The Ministry of the Interior employed a system of informants and CDR block committees to report on suspicious activities.

I also find it implausible that the claimant could have bribed officials of the Ministry of Immigration to get her exit permit by simply giving them perfumes and soaps. A report published by Human Rights Watch (HRW) indicates that Cuban authorities often deny exit permits to citizens who wish to travel abroad, and that the "efforts of those who want to leave to circumvent the restrictions can prove very costly, whether it is the grave dangers faced fleeing the country on the high seas or the exorbitant bribes paid to corrupt officials to arrange travel permits". In addition, HRW's report states that an individual who organizes, promotes, or incites an illegal exit can be punished with two to five years of imprisonment, while someone who provides material assistance, offers information, or in any way facilitates an illegal exit, risks two to five years behind bars.

The claimant said that if the Cuban authorities found out that she was engaged in the illegal production and sale of moonshine and she was forced to return to Cuba that she would face serious consequences. She said that her having been deemed to be politically unreliable, having been fired from her job and blacklisted from finding any future employment, combined with her involvement in illegal employment activities, cumulatively would intensify the consequences and punishment that she would face upon her return to Cuba. The claimant said that she would expect to be tried in regard to all of these offences and that the likely result would be that she would go to prison. The claimant said that she did not know how long she would have to go to prison for and that it would depend to a great extent on what the authorities would perceive her to have done against the communist regime.

The claimant testified that her son returned to Cuba in XXXXX 2010 to visit his grandmother and brother. The claimant testified that upon his return there her son discovered that the Cuban authorities had issued several citations against her. The claimant said that her son brought copies of these citations to Canada to present in support of her claim for protection. The claimant testified that her son found out that the citations were in regards to the claimant having engaged in illegal employment activities. The citations which were produced at the claimant's hearing and entered into evidence as exhibit "C-7" indicate that claimant was required to appear before a tribunal for an oral hearing and that failure on her part to show up would result in the issuance of a warrant for her arrest and detention. However, there is no indication in the citations that the claimant had been charged or was being prosecuted for illegal employment pursuant to the "dangerousness" provisions of the penal code. The claimant said that her son also found out that the other people who had been engaged in the illegal moonshine production business had been charged and were being prosecuted pursuant to the "dangerousness" provisions of the Cuban penal code. The claimant said her son found out that other people who had been involved in illegal employment activities had also been processed under the "dangerousness" provisions of the penal code.

I find that there is no persuasive evidence before me to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has been charged pursuant to the "dangerousness" provisions of the penal code for violating the employment laws of Cuba. I find that the claimant has failed to provide me with sufficient reliable, credible, and probative documentation to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Cuban authorities have commenced prosecution of the claimant for a violation of the employment laws under the "dangerousness" provisions of the penal code in Cuba. Furthermore, I find no persuasive evidence before me to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's friends, who were also involved in the illegal moonshine business, have been charged and are being prosecuted under the "dangerousness" provisions of the penal code in Cuba.

The claimant testified that if she were to return to Cuba, given her failure to show up for an oral hearing as required by the citations, that she would be immediately detained at the airport and that the authorities would commence a legal process against her for having worked illegally in Cuba and for overstaying her visit in Canada beyond the time allotted to her by the Cuban government pursuant to her exit permit. She said the authorities would also punish everyone who helped her in Cuba and that she would be denied a ration card. The claimant said that she would also be processed by the authorities for being politically unreliable and that she would never be permitted to work again.

I find that the claimant's allegation that she would face serious consequences in Cuba amounting to persecution on account of her political profile is not supported by the evidence. Although the claimant was deemed to be politically unreliable by her XXXXX XXXXX in 2000, some 10 years ago, there is no persuasive evidence to show that she continues to be perceived by the authorities either as either politically unreliable or a political dissident who is opposed to the principles of the revolution. I find, had that been the case, it is unlikely that the Cuban regime would have given her an exit permit allowing her to leave the country in 2008. The claimant testified that she believed that the only reason why she was given an exit permit in 2007 was because a friend of hers, a XXXXX XXXXX, had given her a fraudulent employment letter which was all that was needed in order to get approval for an exit permit from the Cuban authorities. The claimant suggested that with such a letter, getting approval for an exit permit was almost guaranteed, because the authorities would not pay attention to anything else. I find the claimant's suggestion to be largely unsubstantiated and speculative.

I respectfully disagree and reject the claimant's inference. I find that it is clear, based on the evidence, that the claimant had a pre-existing record with the Cuban authorities dating back to 2000 when the claimant ran into problems with her XXXXX XXXXX and the Ministry of XXXXX. The claimant was fired because she had been outside of Cuba during the XXXXX XXXXX without proper authorization, had been deemed politically unreliable based on information indicating that she had made statements against the principles of the revolution in the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, and had associated with dissidents in Canada opposed to the revolution in Cuba.

I find that, if the Cuban authorities had truly considered her to be a political dissident, or politically unreliable, or a serious political threat to the principles of the revolution and the Cuban regime, based on the claimant's actions in 2000, it is highly unlikely that they would have granted her an exit permit in 2007, notwithstanding that she had presented a fraudulent employment letter to the authorities in 2007 in order to get her exit permit. (b) Risk of harm under the "Dangerousness" Law

The claimant testified that she feared that she would be prosecuted and imprisoned pursuant to the "dangerousness" laws of Cuba for having worked in an illegal business involving the production and sale of moonshine on the black market. The claimant testified that her son returned to Cuba in 2010 and found out that the other people who worked with her in the illegal underground moonshine business had been charged and were being prosecuted pursuant to the "dangerousness" provisions of the Cuban penal code. The claimant said that her son also found out that the citations that the authorities had issued in her name in Cuba were also in regards to her involvement in the illegal bootlegging business on the black market in Cuba. The claimant said that her son also found out that the authorities were going to prosecute her for her illegal employment in the moonshine business pursuant to the "dangerousness" laws. I reiterate once again that there is no persuasive evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the authorities in Cuba have charged the claimant for illegal employment and intend to prosecute her for working in an illegal moonshine business under the "dangerousness" provisions of the Cuban penal code.

Although I find that the "dangerousness" provisions of the Cuban penal code are overtly political in terms of the wording of the relevant sections of the law and that they have been applied in a persecutory manner against "political dissidents",5 there is no more than a mere possibility that the claimant would be subject to prosecution and imprisonment pursuant to the "dangerousness" provisions for the following reasons.

The claimant said that after she was fired from her position as XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX with the Ministry of XXXXX back in 2000, she was black listed and was unable to find work anywhere despite her persistent efforts between 2000 and 2004. She said that friends of hers who were illegally making rum in their house offered her a job to help them with this illegal business and that she accepted. The claimant testified that she had no choice but to participate in this illegal black market business because it was the only way that she could survive economically since being blacklisted by the communist regime back in 2000. The claimant testified that the authorities knew full well that she was engaged in this illegal business and that they regularly stopped her on the street and searched her bag. She said also that they gave her numerous warnings to stop her activities in the bootlegging business. The claimant said that they warned her if she did not stop her activities they were going to process her legally. The claimant testified that other than stopping her on the street and searching her bag, she was not subjected to any other reprisals or punishment at the hands of the Cuban authorities for being involved in the illegal production and sale of rum on the black market. The claimant said that the Cuban authorities kept looking for proof of her involvement in this illegal business but never found any. The claimant testified that she continued to work in this underground business right up until the time she came to Canada in 2008.

I find that if the Cuban authorities already knew that she was involved in this illegal employment in the bootlegging business and actually considered this to constitute a serious offence under Cuban laws it is unlikely that they would have waited until 2010 to take any concrete steps to have her processed and prosecuted for her activities in the illegal bootlegging operation under the "dangerousness" provisions of the penal code. Additionally, I also find, in light of the documentary evidence, that although the claimant might face threats of being charged or prosecuted for illegal employment under the "dangerousness" laws, it is not likely that the authorities in actual practice would charge and prosecute her under these provisions in regards to her illegal employment. The penal code includes the concept of "potential dangerousness", defined as the "special proclivity of a person to commit crimes, demonstrated by his conduct in manifest contradiction of socialist norms."6 No evidence is required for a conviction for this offense. The Cuban Commission for Human Rights and National Reconciliation (CCDHRN) estimated that between 3,000 and 5,000 citizens were serving time in detention for this offense, including approximately 1,000 women (mostly for suspicion of prostitution). The authorities mostly applied this law in nonpolitical cases to target prostitutes, young person who refused to report to work centres, and repeat offenders of laws restricting change of domicile. During detentions, authorities frequently threatened dissidents with prosecutions for "dangerousness", although few were charged and sentenced.

Further documentary evidence indicates that the Raul Castro government has also increasingly relied on a "dangerousness" provision to imprison individuals who have not committed any crime. This provision has been applied both to dissidents and to ordinary Cubans who are unemployed or illegally self-employed.7 I find that there is no persuasive evidence to show that the "dangerousness" laws are being systematically applied in a widespread fashion to target and punish all ordinary Cubans or Cuban dissidents who have taken up illegal self-employment. Although a Human Rights Watch report8 indicates that Cubans who were unemployed or illegally self-employed were routinely prosecuted for "dangerousness", I find no empirical data to support this finding. Additionally, I find that the report makes contradictory findings. On the one hand, the report says that the government of Raul Castro is "increasingly" relying on the "dangerousness" provisions of the Cuban penal code to imprison dissenters and ordinary Cubans who are unemployed or illegally self-employed, but on the other hand, the report says that Cubans who were unemployed or illegally self-employed were "routinely" prosecuted for "dangerousness". One of the report's findings suggests that there has been a "higher incidence" of resorting to prosecuting dissidents and ordinary Cubans who are unemployed or illegally self-employed under Raul Castro. However, the report makes another finding which suggests that in every instance where a dissident, or ordinary Cuban is unemployed, or illegally self-employed, the government under Raul Castro resorts to prosecution under the "dangerousness" provisions of the Cuban penal code. There is no empirical data in this report to support this finding. The source of this finding are human rights defenders and journalists in Havana, Sancti Spiritus, Holguin, Santiago, and Guantanamo.9 These two conclusions, in my view, are contradictory. Given that the claimant does not fit the profile of non-dissident Cubans who are typically and primarily targeted by means of prosecution under the "dangerousness", namely, prostitutes, young persons refusing to report to work centres, and repeat offenders of laws restricting change of domicile, I find that there is no more than a mere possibility that the claimant would be charged, prosecuted, and punished for illegal self-employment in the black market bootlegging business with her friends, pursuant to the "dangerousness" laws. (c) Risk of harm for violating the Exit Laws of Cuba

The claimant testified that prior to coming to Canada in XXXXX 2008, she obtained a legal exit permit from the Cuban authorities through improper and illegal means. She said that she had a close friend of hers, a XXXXX XXXXX, prepare a fraudulent letter to be presented to officials of the Ministry of XXXXX to facilitate the issuance of an exit permit. I find that there is no persuasive evidence to establish that the Cuban authorities are aware of the fact that the claimant obtained her exit permit through illegal or improper means. The evidence shows that the claimant sought and obtained permission from the Cuban authorities to exit Cuba. The evidence also shows that after entering Canada with an exit permit on XXXXX, 2008, which was valid for a period of 30 days, she intentionally allowed her exit permit to expire and made no efforts to have it extended from abroad in Canada. The claimant said that there was no possibility of doing so while she was in Canada. The claimant's testimony is contradicted by the preponderance of the documentary evidence. According to the documentary evidence, Cubans who are in Canada can extend their exit permits for up to 10 months and 29 days from the date on which the permit holder leaves the country.10 I prefer the evidence found in the documentation over the claimant's testimony because it comes from reliable and reputable objectives sources such as Amnesty International.

Based on the information available, Cuban law prescribes some form of punishment for contravention of exit and entry laws. For example, Cuba's Criminal Code provides that individuals who, without completing legal formalities, leave or take actions in preparation for leaving the national territory can face prison sentences of one to three years in prison. Similarly, individuals who organize, promote, or incite an illegal exit can be punished with two to five years of imprisonment, while someone who provides material assistance, offers information, or in any way facilitates an illegal exit, risks two to five years behind bars.11 Law No. 62 of the Penal Code (Código Penal) of Cuba, Article 135.1, Abandonment of Functions (Abandono de Funciones), states that any civil servant or employee fulfilling a mission in a foreign country who abandons their mission, or completes, or fails to return to Cuba when required, expressly or tacitly, will be deprived of their freedom for three to eight years.12

There is no persuasive evidence that the claimant would be punished for anything other than as is provided for by Cuban law, a law of general application, for having stayed outside Cuba beyond the time allowed. The Federal Court of Appeal in Valentin,13 held: "... Neither the international Convention nor our Act, which is based on it, as I understand it, had in mind the protection of people who, having been subjected to no persecution to date, themselves created a cause to fear persecution by freely, of their own accord and with no reason, making themselves liable to punishment for violating a law of general application. ..."

Having full knowledge of the fact that her exit permit was only valid for 30 days, the claimant knowingly overstayed and violated the terms of her exit visa, then took no actions to properly extend her lawful stay in Canada. Instead, she allowed her exit permit to expire, thereby creating a situation in which she now claims she cannot return as she would face punishment. Law No. 62 of the Cuban Penal Code indicates that loss of freedom for three to eight years can be imposed.14 I have examined the wording of Law No. 62 of the Cuban penal code. I do not find the language used to be overtly political. I find that the Law No. 62 is neither explicitly or implicitly discriminatory or persecutory. Furthermore, I find that the penalty prescribed for violating the exit laws, is neither disproportionately harsh, or excessive in relation to the nature of the offence. As this punishment is a law of general application, I do not find that it constitutes a risk of harm and agree with the Federal Court's finding in Valentin, as not being the intent of refugee protection.

I have also considered whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant, given her past record and problems with the Cuban authorities, would face judicial sanctions amounting to persecution for having overstayed her exit permit and having made a refugee claim in Canada. I find that the claimant would not face such serious consequences. Affidavit evidence15 produced by the claimant's counsel indicates that Cubans who have overstayed their exit permits and made refugee claims and have no history of political activity would not face serious reprisals such as penal code charges and incarceration. I find that the claimant is not a political dissident. She was never involved in any anti-government protests, demonstrations, nor was she a member of any political group opposed to the principles of the Revolution. Although the claimant made some statements in XXXXX that were critical of the government's policy that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX not have the same XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX with the principles of the revolution, she was never subjected to any disciplinary measures by the Ministry of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX during the many years that she XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. I find, given the claimant's lack of involvement in any anti-government activities or movements in Cuba in the past, that the claimant would not face a serious possibility of severe judicial sanctions amounting to persecution for having overstayed her exit permit and for having made a refugee claim in Canada.

I also find that there is no persuasive evidence to suggest that the Cuban authorities have actual knowledge of the fact that the claimant has made a refugee claim in Canada, or that they are likely to find out that she has done so upon her return to Cuba. Counsel produced another affidavit16 outlining the practices and procedures of Canadian officials at the Canadian Embassy in Havana. According to the affidavit, locally engaged Cuban staff working at the Canadian Embassy do share information with the Cuban government. The same affidavit indicates this practice varies from mission to mission. The document also indicates that faxes sent to the Canadian Embassy from Citizenship and Immigration Canada concerning Cubans who have defected, are not generally secure, but it depends on the particular officer who is handling the faxes. The affidavit also says that locally engaged Cuban staff at the Canadian Embassy do have access to emails and that emails are unclassified. The affidavit indicates that if an email goes to locally engaged staff, they would personally deal with it, unless the email went directly to the manager of the Embassy. I find that this affidavit evidence does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that locally engaged Cuban staff working at the Canadian Embassy in Havana routinely and systematically share confidential information, which they have gleaned from faxes or emails, about Cubans who have made refugee claims in Canada to the Cuban authorities. I find, in the particular circumstances of this case, that even if the procedures and practices at the Canadian Embassy in Havana were to give rise to the transmission of confidential information about the claimant's refugee claim to the Cuban authorities, it would not give rise to a serious possibility of persecution given the claimant's lack of any significant political profile or past political activity.

I have also considered whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant, in light of her past problems with the Cuban authorities in 2000, would face severe extra-judicial sanctions amounting to persecution for having overstayed her exit permit and having made a refugee claim in Canada. I find that there is no persuasive evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that members of her family back home in Cuba have faced severe extra-judicial sanctions on account of the claimant having overstayed her exit permit and having made a refugee claim in Canada. Although I accept, based on the affidavit evidence17 referred to above, that the claimant might face discrimination in the form of harassment by the Cuban authorities if she goes back, or might face discrimination in the form of denial of employment, I find that this does not rise to a level of serious harm or persecution. Although the claimant was black listed back in 2000 and could not find employment, she was, nevertheless, able to survive and continue to live in Cuba until she came to Canada and claimed refugee protection in XXXXX 2008.

Therefore, I find the claimant is not a Convention refugee and the claim under section 96 of the IRPA fails. The rest of the analysis of this decision will be under section 97 of the IRPA. Section 97 - Persons in Need of Protection

For the same reasons as outlined above, an examination of the claim under section 97 of the IRPA also fails. I find the claimant has created a sur place refugee situation which did not exist before she lawfully left Cuba, and now faces legal repercussions in her own country as a result of laws of general application.18 Thus the claimant failed to establish that, based on a balance of probabilities, she would personally be subject to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture. Hence the claim fails pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.
Therefore, I find the claimant is not a person in need of protection and the claim under section 97 of the IRPA fails.

The claimant does not have a well-founded fear since there is not a serious possibility of persecution, and she would not be subjected personally, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture, should she return to Cuba. Accordingly, the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The claim is rejected.
